questions.stem: When and where does the picnic take place?
options: On St Valentine's Day 1901, at Hanging Rock in Victoria
On St Valentine's Day 1900, in the Grampians in Victoria
On St Valentine's Day 1900, at Hanging Rock in Victoria
On New Year's Day 1900, at Hanging Rock in Victoria
questions.explanation: Girls from Appleyard College, a boarding school, picnic at Hanging Rock on Valentine's Day 1900, a year before Federation. The date links the story to romance and to the turn of a century.

questions.stem: During the picnic, the party discovers that their only two watches have done something strange. What?
options: Both have stopped at exactly three o'clock
Both have stopped at exactly twelve noon
Both have stopped at the moment the girls vanish
Both show different times from each other
questions.explanation: The two watches stop at noon, well before the girls walk into the rocks. It is the first sign that ordinary time and order do not apply at the Rock.

questions.stem: Who disappears at Hanging Rock?
options: Miranda, Marion, Irma and Miss McCraw
Miranda, Sara, Edith and Mlle de Poitiers
Marion, Edith, Irma and Mrs Appleyard
Miranda, Irma, Sara and Miss Lumley
questions.explanation: Three girls walk into the rocks and do not return, and the mathematics teacher, Miss McCraw, is also missing. Edith comes back alone.

questions.stem: What does Edith do when Miranda, Marion and Irma walk on into the rocks?
options: She falls asleep and wakes the next morning
She goes to fetch Miss McCraw to bring them back
She screams and runs back down the Rock alone
She follows them and is the first to disappear
questions.explanation: The girls move on as if in a trance, ignoring Edith's calls. Terrified, she runs screaming back down. Her account later is confused and fragmentary.

questions.stem: How is Irma found?
options: She walks back to the college alone a week later and knocks at the front door
Mlle de Poitiers dreams of where she is and leads the search party to her
Michael searches the Rock overnight; Albert follows a clue Michael gives him and finds her
A police tracker follows her footprints to a cave on the far side of the Rock
questions.explanation: Michael spends a night on the Rock and is found exhausted, holding a scrap of a dress. Albert goes back to the spot and finds Irma alive, a week after the picnic.

questions.stem: What can Irma remember about what happened on the Rock?
options: Only the red cloud
Only the name of a stranger
Nothing at all
Everything in detail
questions.explanation: Irma has no memory of what happened. The one survivor cannot solve the mystery, which deepens it.

questions.stem: When Irma visits the other girls to say goodbye, what happens?
options: They crowd around her, shouting at her to tell them what happened
They give her flowers and sing a hymn together in memory of the missing girls
They turn their backs on her in silence, on Mrs Appleyard's strict orders
They beg her to stay at the college instead of going to Europe
questions.explanation: The girls surround Irma and demand answers, and the scene becomes hysterical. The school's order is breaking down under the strain of the mystery.

questions.stem: What happens to the school in the weeks after the picnic?
options: The teachers take over and run the college while Mrs Appleyard leads searches
Parents withdraw their daughters and the college falls into scandal and decline
More families enrol their daughters, drawn by the fame the newspapers have given it
The police close the college and move all the girls to a school in Melbourne
questions.explanation: The disappearances bring rumours and newspaper speculation, and families take their daughters away. The college, a symbol of order, begins to fall apart.

questions.stem: Why does Mrs Appleyard tell Sara she must return to the orphanage?
options: Sara's brother has written to ask for her to come home
Sara's guardian has stopped paying her school fees
Sara has been caught trying to run away to the Rock
Sara has refused to take part in the posture lessons
questions.explanation: Sara's guardian has not paid her fees. Mrs Appleyard, worried about money and reputation, turns on the weakest girl in the school.

questions.stem: What happens to Sara?
options: She is found dead in the college greenhouse, after Mrs Appleyard lies about her leaving
She is found alive on Hanging Rock, with no memory of how she came to be there
She is collected by her guardian and leaves the college, never to be heard of again
She runs away to Melbourne and finds work there with the help of her brother Bertie
questions.explanation: Mrs Appleyard claims Sara's guardian collected her, but Sara's body is later found in the greenhouse. The film does not show how she died, but the lie points to Mrs Appleyard's guilt.

questions.stem: How does the film end?
options: Miranda returns to the college and explains to the police what happened
Michael finds the remains of the missing girls in a hidden cave high on the Rock
Mrs Appleyard confesses that she knows where the girls have gone
A voiceover says the mystery has never been solved, over images of the picnic
questions.explanation: The voiceover reports Mrs Appleyard's death at the Rock and says the girls and Miss McCraw were never found. The film ends with the picnic, as if still frozen in that day.

questions.stem: How is Miranda presented in the film?
options: As a shy, plain girl whom the others tease and leave out of their games
As a sickly girl who stays behind at the college on the day of the picnic
As a serene, beautiful girl whom the others adore, compared to a Botticelli angel
As a rebellious girl who is often punished by Mrs Appleyard for breaking the rules
questions.explanation: Mlle de Poitiers compares Miranda to an angel painted by Botticelli. She seems almost otherworldly, which makes her disappearance feel like a mystery rather than a crime.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Mrs Appleyard?
options: A strict headmistress, obsessed with reputation, who grows harsher as the school fails
A kind, motherly headmistress who comforts the girls and leads the search for the missing
A young headmistress who secretly sympathises with the girls who disappeared
A grief-stricken headmistress who blames herself and softens towards the girls
questions.explanation: Mrs Appleyard cares most about the college's reputation and money. As families leave, she becomes more vindictive rather than gentler, and her cruelty to Sara has terrible results.

questions.stem: What contrast does the film draw between Michael Fitzhubert and Albert Crundall?
options: Michael is Miranda's brother; Albert is engaged to Mrs Appleyard's niece
Michael is a refined young Englishman; Albert is a blunt, working-class Australian
Michael is a young police officer from Melbourne; Albert is a teacher at the college
Michael is a local farmer's son; Albert is a visiting English aristocrat
questions.explanation: Michael, nephew of the wealthy Fitzhuberts, is shy and genteel; Albert works for the family and speaks his mind. Their friendship crosses the class lines of colonial society.

questions.stem: What does Miranda tell Sara before the picnic?
options: That Sara should write a poem about the picnic to read to the class later
That Sara must learn to love someone else, because Miranda won't be there much longer
That Sara must stay behind, because Mrs Appleyard has forbidden her to come on the picnic
That Sara will be the one to find her if she ever becomes lost on the Rock
questions.explanation: Sara, an orphan, adores Miranda. Miranda's gentle warning seems to foreshadow her disappearance, and it leaves Sara even more alone.

questions.stem: Albert dreams that Sara visits him to say goodbye and calls him 'Bertie'. What does the film suggest?
options: That Albert is mistaken, and Sara has really run away to find Miranda
That Albert is the brother Sara lost when they were separated as orphans
That Albert has secretly fallen in love with Sara and plans to marry her one day
That Albert knows where Miranda is and wants Sara to tell the police
questions.explanation: Sara grieves for her lost brother Bertie, and Bertie can be short for Albert. Neither of them knows the other is so close, which adds to the film's sense of loss.

questions.stem: What does Mlle de Poitiers discover about Miss Lumley and Sara?
options: Miss Lumley has strapped Sara to a wall, claiming to correct her posture
Miss Lumley has been helping Sara write secret letters to her lost brother Bertie
Miss Lumley has been paying Sara's school fees out of her own wages
Miss Lumley has locked Sara in the greenhouse as a punishment
questions.explanation: The scene shows the cruelty and control behind the college's genteel manners. The warm French teacher is shocked; the school's discipline is aimed at the weakest girl.

questions.stem: Picnic at Hanging Rock is based on a novel by which author?
options: Patrick White
Joan Lindsay
Miles Franklin
Henry Lawson
questions.explanation: Joan Lindsay published the novel in 1967. Peter Weir's film, written by Cliff Green, follows its story but is a work in its own right.

questions.stem: Is Picnic at Hanging Rock based on a true story?
options: No, and the film opens by telling the audience the story is invented
No, but the film's opening presents the events as if they really happened
Yes, the film uses police records of three girls who vanished in 1900
Yes, Joan Lindsay was a pupil at the college and saw the girls disappear
questions.explanation: Hanging Rock is real, but the story is fiction. The opening title gives a date and place as if reporting history, and many viewers came to believe it was true.

questions.stem: Why is the film important in Australian film history?
options: It was the first Australian film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture
It was the first Australian feature film to be made with government funding
It launched Peter Weir's career, as it was the very first feature film he directed
Its success helped bring world attention to the Australian New Wave of the 1970s
questions.explanation: The film was a hit at home and abroad, and helped draw international attention to a new wave of Australian filmmaking. Weir had already directed The Cars That Ate Paris, and other government-funded features came before it. It has often been voted among the best Australian films.

questions.stem: The film's look was influenced by the Heidelberg School, such as Frederick McCubbin's painting Lost. What does this connection suggest?
options: It signals that the film is mainly about art and the lives of painters
It ties the film to Australian art about settlers' unease in the bush
It shows that the film was shot in the same place as the painting
It presents the bush as a gentle, nostalgic place of settler pride
questions.explanation: Heidelberg School painters such as McCubbin painted the bush in soft light, and Lost shows a child lost in it. The film borrows that soft light but draws out the tradition's fear of being swallowed by the land rather than its national pride.

questions.stem: How does the 1900 setting add to the film's meaning?
options: English manners and corsets look out of place in the ancient Australian bush
The girls are excited about Federation and plan a parade to celebrate it
A long drought has forced the families of the district off their farms
The gold rush has brought crowds of strangers to the area around the Rock
questions.explanation: The college tries to be a piece of England: tight corsets, gloves and strict manners. Set against the vast, ancient Rock, that imported order looks fragile.

questions.stem: Joan Lindsay's original final chapter, which hinted at an explanation, was cut before the novel was published. How does this relate to the film?
options: The film includes the cut chapter, so it solves the mystery the novel leaves open
The film was made after the cut chapter was published, and it uses that ending
The film adds a new ending in which the police find and arrest a suspect
Like the published novel, the film leaves the disappearances unexplained
questions.explanation: The cut chapter was only published in 1987, after Lindsay's death and long after the film. Weir's film keeps the mystery open, offering possibilities rather than answers.

questions.stem: Which conflict is most central to the film?
options: Imported European order against the ancient, indifferent Australian landscape
Settlers against the Aboriginal owners who resist their claim to the land
Police in Melbourne against bushrangers hiding in the hills around the Rock
Science and reason against the girls' belief in the local legends about the Rock
questions.explanation: The college, with its rules, clocks and corsets, stands for colonial order. The Rock, millions of years old, ignores it. The disappearances expose how little control that order has; no Aboriginal characters or local legends appear in the film.

questions.stem: How does the film connect the disappearances with growing up?
options: The girls are taken because they refuse to leave childhood behind and grow up
The girls shed shoes and stockings on the Rock, escaping the restrictions placed on them
The girls vanish because their teachers force them to grow up too quickly
The girls vanish as a punishment for disobeying a teacher's order to stay together
questions.explanation: The college binds the girls in corsets and rules. On the Rock they loosen them, and Irma is found without her corset. The film links the mystery to young women breaking free of restriction.

questions.stem: How does the film treat the mystery of what happened?
options: It suggests clearly that Michael and Albert were responsible for the crime
It reveals that Miss McCraw led the girls away to start a new life elsewhere
It refuses to solve it, offering possibilities that range from ordinary to mystical
It solves it in the final scene, when Irma's lost memory of the Rock finally returns
questions.explanation: The film hints at accident, crime and something supernatural, but chooses none. The lack of an answer is the point: some things cannot be explained or controlled.

questions.stem: How does the film use time as an idea?
options: A countdown builds suspense until the search party reaches the Rock
Scenes are shown out of order so the audience must piece them together
Stopped watches set human clock time against the Rock's vast age
Flashbacks show the girls' childhoods before they came to the college
questions.explanation: The watches stop at noon and Miranda speaks of things ending at the right time. Human schedules mean nothing to a rock millions of years old.

questions.stem: How did cinematographer Russell Boyd create the film's soft, dreamlike look?
options: By printing the film on grainy, faded stock after filming
By shooting through a lens smeared with petroleum jelly
By placing bridal veil fabric over the camera lens
By filming most scenes through thick morning fog at dawn
questions.explanation: Boyd and Weir stretched fine veil fabric over the lens to soften the image, rather than relying on fog, film stock or smearing the lens. The haze makes the picnic look like a memory or a dream.

questions.stem: Which instrument plays the film's famous haunting theme?
options: The pan flute
The tin whistle
The didgeridoo
The trumpet
questions.explanation: Gheorghe Zamfir's pan flute gives the music an eerie, otherworldly sound. It plays as the girls make their way toward the Rock.

questions.stem: How is the Rock often filmed, and with what effect?
options: Through the windows of the college, so it seems a remote, distant threat
From low, wide angles at its base, so it towers over the people below
From a helicopter high above, so it looks small and harmless
In long shots from far away, so it blends into the distant hills
questions.explanation: Low, wide-angle shots make the Rock loom, tall and close rather than distant. It seems to watch the characters, almost as if it were alive.

questions.stem: As the girls climb toward the monoliths, some shots are in slow motion while Edith is shown at normal speed. What is the effect?
options: It shows the girls are in a trance, cut off from Edith's ordinary world
It shows that Edith is a stronger, faster climber than the others
It shows the girls are injured and can only climb very slowly
It shows Edith's panic, as time seems to slow down for her alone
questions.explanation: Slow motion makes the girls' movement dreamlike, as if they are under a spell. Edith, at normal speed, is left behind in the everyday world; it is the girls, not Edith, whose time seems to slow.

questions.stem: How does the soundtrack build tension as the girls disappear?
options: Thunder and heavy rain drown out the sound of the girls' voices
Layers of insects, birds and a low, hollow groan from the Rock build up
The pan flute theme swells to a loud, triumphant climax
Complete silence falls, broken only by the girls' loud, echoing laughter
questions.explanation: Natural sounds mix with an eerie, windy groan that grows stronger when the camera holds on the Rock. The sound makes the landscape feel threatening rather than triumphant.

questions.stem: In the opening, the Rock is half hidden by mist and never shown whole. What does this suggest?
options: That the Rock is mysterious and can never be fully seen or understood
That the Rock is a gentle, protective presence watching over the girls
That the Rock is unimportant compared with the college and its people
That the story is set in a cold, misty Victorian winter
questions.explanation: Hiding the Rock makes it a mystery from the first images, and the picnic itself takes place on a hot February day. Like the disappearances, the Rock is never presented clearly or completely.

questions.stem: Michael has visions of a white swan. What does the swan represent?
options: Mrs Appleyard, who is watching over him
Irma, who he hopes will soon marry him
Albert, whose friendship he now values
Miranda, whose beauty and loss haunt him
questions.explanation: Michael glimpsed Miranda only briefly at the creek, but she obsesses him. The graceful white swan stands for her, pure and out of reach.

questions.stem: When Irma returns to say goodbye, she wears red while the other girls wear white. What does the costume suggest?
options: That Irma has been changed by the Rock and no longer belongs among them
That Irma has been made head girl of the college, taking Miranda's place
That Irma is in mourning for Miranda, Marion and Miss McCraw
That Irma has been punished by Mrs Appleyard for leaving the group
questions.explanation: White has marked the girls' innocence since the picnic. Irma's red sets her apart: she has passed through something the others can't understand, and they turn on her.

questions.stem: Who speaks the opening line, 'What we see and what we seem are but a dream, a dream within a dream.'?
options: Mrs Appleyard, in her speech before the picnic
Michael, in his dream on the night on the Rock
Mlle de Poitiers, reading poetry to her class
Miranda, in voiceover at the start of the film
questions.explanation: The line, adapted from Edgar Allan Poe's poem 'A Dream within a Dream', is whispered over the opening. It warns that the film will blur dream and reality.

questions.stem: Miranda says, 'Everything begins and ends at exactly the right time and place.' When does she say it, and what does it suggest?
options: On the Rock, before she disappears; she accepts what is about to happen
At the college, before the picnic; she wants the girls to leave on time
To Sara, as she says goodbye; she is promising to return the next day
To Michael, at the creek; she is telling him to forget about her
questions.explanation: Miranda says this calmly high on the Rock, shortly before walking into the rocks. Her words suggest a sense of fate, as if the disappearance is meant to be.

questions.stem: Albert tells Michael, 'I say the crude things, you just think 'em.' What does the line show?
options: Albert's fear that Michael will tell the police what he saw at the creek
Albert's blunt honesty, and the class gap between the two young men
Albert's anger at Michael for taking credit for finding Irma
Albert's envy of Michael's English education and wealthy family
questions.explanation: After Albert makes a crude remark about the girls, he points out that Michael is thinking the same thing. The working-class Australian says what the polite Englishman hides.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest topic sentence for the prompt 'Picnic at Hanging Rock suggests that the Australian landscape cannot be tamed.' Discuss.
options: Picnic at Hanging Rock is a 1975 film directed by Peter Weir and set in Victoria
This essay will discuss the landscape in the film Picnic at Hanging Rock
The girls go on a picnic to Hanging Rock on Valentine's Day in the year 1900
Weir presents the Rock as an ancient force that exposes colonial order as fragile
questions.explanation: A strong topic sentence takes a position on the prompt and names what the paragraph will prove. The others retell, announce or state facts without making an argument.

questions.stem: A student writes: 'The watches stop at twelve o'clock.' How could this be turned into analysis?
options: Add the quotation in which Miranda says everything ends at the right time
Retell what happens after the watches stop, as the girls climb the Rock
Explain how the stopped watches show human time losing its power at the Rock
Name the technique, a symbol, and say that it is an effective one
questions.explanation: Analysis explains what the evidence suggests. Naming a technique, adding a quotation or retelling the plot does not do this; linking the stopped watches to the clash between human order and the ancient landscape turns a detail into an argument.
